SPRING!

subsubtopic: SECOND SESSION-TWENTY-EIGHTH PARLIAMENT 19 ELIZABETH II VOLUME V, 1970 COMPRISING THE PERIOD FROM THE FIFTH DAY OF MARCH, 1970, TO THE TWENTY-FIFTH DAY OF MARCH, 1970, INCLUSIVE. INDEX ISSUED IN A SEPARATE VOLUME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of utmost urgent importance. It has to do with a meteorological and horticultural phenomenon occurring at this very moment on the west coast of this nation, in the province of British Columbia. Evidence of this approaching event was delivered into our hands today as British Columbia members, aided by the Greater Vancouver Visitors and Convention Bureau, provided each and every member of this House with his own sample for study and contemplation.
What I am about to announce, Mr. Speaker, will bring joy to all our hearts, locked as we are in the apparently inexhaustible grip of winter. Spring has shown itself on the Pacific coast! There is absolutely no doubt about it. Daffodils and crocuses are blooming in profusion in greater Vancouver, Burnaby, the Fraser Valley, in the Islands of the Gulf of Georgia and in the gardens on Vancouver Island. If this can happen in British Columbia, it can happen in the rest of Canada. Let us not lose hope.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ambrose Hubert Peddle (Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador):
subtopic: MR. PEDDLE-PRIOR ANNOUNCEMENT OUTSIDE HOUSE OF SETTLEMENT OF TRADE DISPUTE WITH MEXICO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a rather unserious setting for a serious piece of business. I rise on a question of privilege. I intend to follow my few brief remarks with a motion. On Thursday, February 26, I directed a question to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce regarding a trade dispute between Canada and Mexico which threatened to have a very grave economic effect on the newsprint industry in the riding which I
represent. I was assured by the minister that negotiations to resolve the dispute were to take place and that the House would be kept informed.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
At 2 p.m. yesterday, March 4, the Secretary of State for External Affairs tabled in the House an announcement of a settlement of the dispute, and copies were quite properly provided to the Press Gallery after it had been made. However, the announcement was released to the Newfoundland press by the Minister of Transport at approximately ten o'clock yesterday morning, four hours previously.

subtopic: MR. PEDDLE-PRIOR ANNOUNCEMENT OUTSIDE HOUSE OF SETTLEMENT OF TRADE DISPUTE WITH MEXICO
speechtext: Shame!

subtopic: MR. PEDDLE-PRIOR ANNOUNCEMENT OUTSIDE HOUSE OF SETTLEMENT OF TRADE DISPUTE WITH MEXICO
speechtext:
The Minister of Transport acted quite improperly, in my opinion. He used his office to obtain information which, for political reasons, he released some four hours before it was made available to this House. I, and a number of my hon. friends, continued to deal with the numerous expressions of concern from my constituents right up to the opening of the House yesterday, with no way of knowing that the question had been resolved. A minister of the Crown was aware that a settlement had been reached and had announced it publicly four hours previously, extracted his pound of political flesh and clapped his hands gleefully.
There are a number of other serious implications in the fact that this news was released in one province of Canada four hours before it was released in the nine other provinces; I need not go into detail as to that aspect. My motion, seconded by my hon. friend from Gander-Twillingate, if necessary, is that the matter be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.

subtopic: MR. PEDDLE-PRIOR ANNOUNCEMENT OUTSIDE HOUSE OF SETTLEMENT OF TRADE DISPUTE WITH MEXICO
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. PEDDLE-PRIOR ANNOUNCEMENT OUTSIDE HOUSE OF SETTLEMENT OF TRADE DISPUTE WITH MEXICO
speechtext:
The hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador has filed the notice required by the Standing Order. The Chair has thus had an opportunity to consider the circumstances on which the hon. member's question is based.
As he has explained, there had been an undertaking by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce that the House would be kept informed of developments concerning
4402	COMMONS
Settlement of Trade Dispute with Mexico the imposition of a surcharge on certain textiles entering Canada. Such information was conveyed to the House yesterday, pursuant to the minister's undertaking. The difficulty stems from the fact that prior to the tabling of the press release on the subject, the Minister of Transport had made an announcement outside the House.
In so far as the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce is concerned, his undertaking seems to have been met by the tabling of the announcement at the opening of yesterday's session. The question is whether the prior announcement by a minister constitutes a breach of privilege.
I have on occasion referred hon. members to Citation 113 of Beauchesne and also to the views expressed by Sir Erskine May at page 45 of the 17th edition of the author's book on parliamentary practice. Without going into the details of these citations, I would remind hon. members that parliamentary privilege is the sum of the fundamental rights of the House and of its individual members over and above the common law rights of other citizens. Seen in this light, parliamentary privilege or the breach thereof cannot be claimed lightly. Indeed, Citation 113 of Beauchesne states specifically that a question of privilege ought rarely to come up in Parliament.
In the same citation, Beauchesne suggests that such a question should be dealt with by a motion giving the House power to impose a reparation, or impose a remedy. What reparation or what remedy would result from a referral of this question to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections or any other committee of the House is difficult to see.
It seems to me that the only action which could be taken would be to condemn the action of the minister, and this, I suggest, can only be done by way of a substantive motion. Again, there are many precedents to support this suggestion. My conclusion is that although the hon. member may have a grievance, or may wish to question the propriety of the minister's early announcement, there is not a prima facie case of privilege which should be investigated by a committee.
I should add that perhaps the kind of situation or circumstances to which the hon. member has alluded might very well be the subject of debate under the motion standing in the name of the Leader of the Opposition which will be considered by the House later today.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF RATIFICATION OF NUCLEAR NON-PROLIFERATION TREATY BY CERTAIN NATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take a few minutes of the time of the House in order to welcome an historic development marking the most important achievement to date in the field of arms control. I refer to the ceremony in Washington this morning and to the similar ceremony in Moscow today during which instruments of ratification of the nuclear non-proliferation treaty are being deposited by the United
March 5, 1970	COMMONS
States, the Soviet Union and a sufficient number of other states to bring the treaty into force.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF RATIFICATION OF NUCLEAR NON-PROLIFERATION TREATY BY CERTAIN NATIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF RATIFICATION OF NUCLEAR NON-PROLIFERATION TREATY BY CERTAIN NATIONS
speechtext:
This convention is the culmination of more than five years of negotiations in which Canada played a significant role. Canada ratified the treaty on January 8, 1969 and was in fact the first nation with a technological capacity to produce nuclear weapons to renounce this weapons option by ratifying the non-proliferation treaty. We shall continue to stress the importance of adherence to the treaty by those states that already have or are close to attaining the technological capacity to produce nuclear weapons-the so-called "near-nuclear" nations.
Canada welcomes the coming into force of this treaty and urges all countries to make it an effective means of counteracting the dangers inherent in the proliferation of nuclear weapons. We hope that those nations which have signed the treaty but not yet ratified it, as well as those which have not yet signed, will proceed to ratification and to implement its safeguards provisions designed to preclude proliferation. Finally, we hope and expect that, in accordance with Article VI of the treaty, this substantial step forward will inspire renewed efforts to curtail the arms race.

speakeroldname: Hon. Roberi L. Sianfield (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF RATIFICATION OF NUCLEAR NON-PROLIFERATION TREATY BY CERTAIN NATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to associate myself with the remarks of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. This is a very significant day. While we must, of course, bear in mind, as I am sure we will -indeed, this announcement constitutes a reminder to us-how much yet remains to be done before we can feel that we really have effective control of nuclear weapons or their proliferation in the world, nevertheless this is a step about which we can be very pleased.
I think it is appropriate, as we welcome this development, to bear in mind not only the effort made by the present Secretary of State for External Affairs but also those of his predecessors, going back to the days of the Hon. Howard Green, all of whom were concerned about atomic weapons and their proliferation. Neither must we forget the efforts of the devoted officials of the Department of External Affairs. As I say, I am happy today to associate myself with the remarks of the minister.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Leader of the N.D.P.
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF RATIFICATION OF NUCLEAR NON-PROLIFERATION TREATY BY CERTAIN NATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is, of course, true that every citizen in every part of the world will be happy to hear that the non-proliferation treaty has at last been ratified by a sufficient number of states to bring it into force. I join with the Leader of the Opposition and the Secretary of State for External Affairs in greeting the importance of this event.
I am sure I am not saying anything more than is in the hearts and minds of every member of this House when I warn that we should not become too complacent about this treaty, first, because it touches a matter which is not as basic to the problem of the nuclear arms threat as some other matters; second, because important nations in the world have not ratified the treaty, one of them being France and another China, so that the family of nations under this treaty is still very dangerously incomplete and, third, this treaty, like the test ban treaty, only touches the periphery of the problem of the threat of the nuclear destruction of humanity. It merely indicates the need for further steps and discussions in SALT and at the disarmament conference in Geneva.
In brief, while I join everybody else in greeting the importance of this day, I am conscious of the fact that it is a small and relatively less important step toward relieving the world of the danger of nuclear destruction, than the very important and much more difficult steps that lie ahead.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF RATIFICATION OF NUCLEAR NON-PROLIFERATION TREATY BY CERTAIN NATIONS

are glad to endorse the comments made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. We rejoice at this historic event which is the most important accomplishment so far in the field of arms control.

Mr. Speaker, Canada stands as a shining example for humanity, because this treaty will certainly help men refrain from killing each other, as could easily have been the case.
It is with pleasure therefore that we join the government and the leaders of the other parties in welcoming this achievement.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: STATEMENT ON CONDITIONS IN TORONTO OFFICE
speechtext:
On Monday, Mr. Speaker, at the suggestion of the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings and the hon. member for Greenwood, I agreed to make a statement in the House today to ascertain whether or not there was any delay in the servicing of unemployment insurance claims in the Toronto area. The hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings mentioned that such a delay would be due to the rapid rise in unemployment in Metropolitan Toronto, while the hon. member for Greenwood was concerned about the long delays and queues which have accumulated in the Toronto office. He suggested special measures including a larger staff and more interpreters.
The answer, as supplied to me by the Unemployment Insurance Commission, is very detailed and very lengthy, and in view of the fact that the estimates of the Unemployment Insurance Commission will be before the appropriate committee in a very short time I would like to reserve this lengthy statement until that time. Nevertheless, I think it is fair to both hon. gentlemen that I touch briefly on some of the contents of this statement.
The Unemployment Insurance Commission points out that the volume of payment of
[Mr. Caouette.l
unemployment insurance tends to increase during the winter months because of seasonal lay-offs in various industries. As the pattern is a repeating one, the Unemployment Insurance Commission plans its workload accordingly and it is wrong to imply that increased workloads in winter are unforeseen and unplanned. Since January, 1970, the increase in new claims over the comparable months last year was under 700. The active claims increased by a little more than 8,000. In anticipation of this increased work load the Unemployment Insurance Commission increased its normal complement of 330 regular employees by 130 seasonal employees. This is approximately 50 more than last year.
The hon. member for Greenwood pointed out the inconvenience and the hardship of queues in long lines at the UIC office. In order to reduce these long line-ups the UIC recently added a telephone service in order to avoid the necessity of people coming to the office, sometimes at great inconvenience to these people. There are at present 16 telephone lines to handle incoming calls only and an additional 10 lines to handle outgoing inquiry calls. There are also 80 other telephones in the Toronto office. It may be useful to note that the total inquiries by telephone and in person are in fact lower this January than a year ago.
In the case of the line-ups, members may recall that before the UIC introduced service by mail the larger Toronto offices would handle 6,000 to 7,000 personal callers per day necessitating line-ups that extended out onto the street and around the corner. Now, under the postal system, calls to the office number 500 to 600 on peak days, or approximately 70 to 80 per hour. Last week when a press photographer called at the office to take a picture of people waiting in line, he left without photographs because there were fewer than ten people waiting in line, and he felt that this did not dramatize it in the way intended.
The necessary forms that must be completed by claimants have been greatly improved and more than half the questions on the forms are questions related to identification of the claimant. Furthermore, the commission has recently revised a great number of form letters in order that the language be made less technical and more easily understandable to everyone.
Most inquiries arise because claimants fail to qualify because of insufficient contributions
March 5, 1970

or employment in non-insurable employment and not because of commission delays.
In short, people are now able to deal with the UIC by mailing in their forms which, if properly filled out, result in speedy payment, also by mail. In addition, callers no longer have to come to the office to make personal inquiries. Those who report to the office do so voluntarily to obtain general information.
Forms are available at the Post Office, Canada Manpower Centres and in some union halls.
I should like to shorten this statement. Statistics kept by the commission indicate that claimants are paid consistently within three weeks of the date of initial claim for 97 per cent or more of claims. This is an even higher proportion than last year. For example, on January 12 only 2.8 per cent of the claims filed in the third previous week were still pending and only 12 claims of 4,458 were still pending from the fourth previous week.
I have other similar statistics which I shall skip over. On February 23, the last total I have, only 1.6 per cent were unsettled at the end of three weeks and 6 of 6,407 were pending from the fourth previous week.
Both official languages are available to claimants in the Toronto office. In addition, several of the employees speak a number of the more common languages in the Toronto area. Efforts will be made to identify these employees in order to facilitate the problems of new Canadians who are not yet fully conversant in either of the official languages. It is not unusual for 10 to 12 languages to be spoken at one time or another by claimants, admittedly creating a problem in communication. Nevertheless, the commission has always been ready to do what it can to secure help in interpretation as required.
Several information publications are now being written in several languages to assist in educating insured persons concerning unemployment insurance requirements and how to go about filing and receiving unemployment insurance.
[DOT] (2:30 p.m.)
The Toronto office is presently located on Dufferin Street in temporary premises. It is the intention of the commission to split into two separate offices in the area of Toronto, one of which will be located on St. Clair Avenue and the other in the west end of the city. This will be done before next winter.
Unemployment Insurance Office Conditions
I have already arranged for the physical facilities of UIC offices across the country to be made more comfortable for applicants and the general public visiting these offices.
In conclusion, I would like to emphasize again that the UIC is perfectly capable of coping with current workloads of claims. Both its staff and its systems are such that they can meet any emergency which may arise because of particular circumstances in an industry or an area. There will always be cases where for lack of complete records or particular circumstances, such as for one claim following a previous claim, a longer time is required to process the payments. These cases are serious for the people affected and everything possible is being done to minimize this problem.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON CONDITIONS IN TORONTO OFFICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we appreciate the statement the minister has just made concerning conditions in the Unemployment Insurance Commission office in Toronto. I also thank the minister for sending me a copy of the statement.
The very fact that there is an increase of 700 new claims and of 8,000 active claims over the figures in the same month a year ago illustrates the serious unemployment situation in Toronto. I cannot understand nor, I am sure, can the people of Toronto, why a city the size of Metropolitan Toronto has only one unemployment insurance office and that a temporary office on Dufferin Street. Surely a city the size of Toronto needs at least two offices, and I am glad the minister is making arrangements to open a second office. However, here we are locking the door after the horse has been stolen. This should have been done long ago for a city the size of Toronto.
The office of the UIC is doing much to relieve the serious situation. We are glad to hear that more telephones have been installed and we are pleased to learn that new forms have been introduced. The forms which claimants have had to complete in the past could only be figured out by a Philadelphia lawyer. Too many questions were put in too small a space poked full of holes for computers purposes. In many cases the holes went through the words printed on the cards, which made questions difficult to understand. No wonder people had all kinds of trouble in filling out these forms. I am glad the minister has revised them.
The minister said that only a small percentage of applicants have not had their unemployment insurance claims paid. The percentage may be small but the number of people is

subtopic: STATEMENT ON CONDITIONS IN TORONTO OFFICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am naturally delighted at the minister's announcement which indicates a sensitive reaction to the criticism by members of the opposition of the situation which has developed in regard to unemployment insurance in light of the very substantially increased numbers of unemployed. I think the figure is over 30 per cent in Metropolitan Toronto, which indicates a much larger increase than the usual seasonal one.
It seems to me it is of the utmost importance in this as in other fields where the individual citizen confronts the state or its representatives that he be assured that his rights and his feelings are being treated with respect. Justice should not only be done but should be seen to be done. Employment in today's world is so important, both to the maintenance of income and to the maintenance of self-respect, that unemployment is a traumatic experience.
In the past, as I know very well myself and as the minister's statement indicated, unemployed people have been subjected to delay, frustration and discomfort because of their difficulties in completing forms, in attending inadequately staffed offices and in having to wait in line and often to return from time to time. There are other problems such as transportation which may seem small but are serious when there is only one small office for a vast area like Metropolitan Toronto. These problems will have to be considered.
I am very pleased that steps have been taken and are being taken to remedy the


situation, and I sincerely hope they will be effective.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON CONDITIONS IN TORONTO OFFICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are also pleased with the measures that have just been announced by the Minister of Labour who is responsible for Unemployment Insurance offices.
Many members have been aware of the problems concerning unemployment insurance for a long time. We are happy to learn that the minister is ready to take the necessary steps in order to make the application forms for benefits understandable to citizens of various ethnic groups who have to deal with Unemployment Insurance offices.
However, the statement made me realize as it did for the previous speakers that the problems about unemployment insurance are increasing because of technical reasons, but also because of the present economic conditions in Canada. In fact, the Minister of Labour can improve the methods, personnel and working conditions in the Unemployment Insurance offices with a view to providing better services to the claimants; however, if the economic conditions deteriorate before the department has been able to achieve the proposed improvements, we will keep on losing ground.
I must also recognize that the Unemployment Insurance Commission, the subject dealt with by the minister just now, has installed long-distance telephone systems in some cities, in order to allow the claimants to describe their problems more readily to UIC officials.
Besides, UIC officials have told us that the Department went too fast in establishing a Canada-wide system of computers in regional offices, particularly in larger centers such as Montreal which covers the whole province of Quebec.
They say also that the computer system was initiated prematurely and in too many places at once, instead of limiting it to one region in order to detect its flaws and then confidently establishing it in the other regions.
Before closing, Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the minister to see that the computers operate as soon as possible in order that the thousands of claims which have been pending for weeks or months may be settled.
March 5, 1970

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATION-EFFECT OF ALLEGED ARBITRARY ACTIONS AND DESTRUCTIVE POLICIES OF SECRECY AND NON-DISCLOSURE
speechtext:
That this House condemns the government for Its arbitrary actions and destructive policies of secrecy and non-disclosure including its attitude towards parliament which deny the right of citizens in this [Mr. Macdonald (Rosedale) .1
country to be informed and to participate fully in the government of Canada, particularly through their elected representatives, and which endanger the balance between the two structures of government-the executive and the representative.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am sorry that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is out of the city today because, by the very nature of things, this resolution touches the Prime Minister closely as head of the government. I think I should begin by quoting one of the Prime Minister's favourite authorities in politics. In the 16th century Machiavelli wrote:
-our experience has been that those princes who have done great things have held good faith of little account, and have known how to circumvent the intellect of men by craft, and in the end have overcome those who have relied on their word.
It is in light of this quotation that I wish to consider some developments that have taken place in Canada during the past year or two, developments which, taken together, I suggest are quite alarming. It seems to me that all the talk that there has been about participatory democracy has been only a screen to hide the effort to concentrate power in Canada and to weaken our traditional safeguards against the abuse of power.
Over the past couple of years there has been a gradual but quite radical change in the system of government in Canada, with an almost invisible and ad hoc amendment of our constitution, so as to build up the power of the office of the Prime Minister and of the cabinet of Canada and to break down institutional safeguards designed to protect the individual Canadian. While not wishing to be in any way an alarmist, I do suggest that a pattern has emerged which requires the attention of the Canadian public, certainly the attention of Parliament, and not least the attention of private members on the other side of the House in whose name the cabinet is accumulating this power.
I ask this House to consider some of the elements of this dangerous, and I think undemocratic, concentration of power at the centre of government in this country. The changes in Parliament are well known, and they are very crucial. They are well known because Parliament must always be the ultimate protection of the individual against an arbitrary government. The issue goes way beyond Parliament and should be discussed in its broader terms as well, that is, in terms broader than Parliament, important as that is, because Parliament is the most important
March 5, 1970	COMMONS
safeguard of citizens. They have other safeguards which have lost a lot of their clout during the last two years.
I have suggested that the talk about participation is simply talk. After all, there is a big difference between genuine participatory democracy which is, on the one hand, to send up trial balloons to sample public opinion and, on the other hand, an exercise in public relations designed to condition the public to a change that the government has already decided to make. There is also a difference between participatory discussions and shouting matches with extremists; the latter may very well be designed to suggest that all of those who disagree with the government are also extremists.

This is a well known technique which was not invented by the Prime Minister, (Mr. Trudeau) but employed to a considerable extent by him.
During the 1960's, governments representing both parties established various new agencies and new programs genuinely designed to broaden the base of government and participation in government, to broaden the opportunity for citizens to express their views or draw attention to their demands. These were genuine examples of participatory democracy. It is very interesting and noteworthy to consider that their fate is in the hands of this government.
The ARDA program, with its emphasis on community involvement in decision making, is certainly being pushed out. Perhaps the best example of its replacement was the Prince Edward Island development plan where the effective control is highly centralized here in Ottawa.
Then there is the Company of Young Canadians. Certainly, it has been "co-opted" and turned into what looks like a tamed creature of the government. We all agree about the government's role as an agent. We, on this side of the House, would have wished the government to start afresh. Certainly, Sir, we never agreed to an agency designed to be participatory being simply taken over and operated by the government. The mandate of this agency now is to be an agent of the government among the young, and not an agency of youth in governmental matters. This distinction is generically the same as the distinction between propaganda and information.

It is clear that at the same time the government is talking about making democracy work, it is changing or restricting or closing down those few federal agencies which have allowed some form of genuine participation. These programs have been replaced by tokenism; for example, naming regional representatives of the poor and flying them occasionally to Ottawa for discussion.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATION-EFFECT OF ALLEGED ARBITRARY ACTIONS AND DESTRUCTIVE POLICIES OF SECRECY AND NON-DISCLOSURE
speechtext:
I suggest there has been quite an alarming increase in the recourse of this government to arbitrary procedures. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) has left the House, and I am sorry he has. According to reports, that minister directly threatened to impose or continue certain policies against copper companies unless they agreed to limitations on price increases. We can all understand the desire to curb price increases or to limit them if they cannot be avoided. The suggestion is that the minister concerned boasted of the big stick he holds over the producers by way of copper export permits.
There is also the whole question of sanctions and the government's proposed voluntary restraint program. I favour this program and I have been advocating the use of guidelines. I must say that I am concerned about the cloak and dagger methods the government seems to be resorting to in order to obtain compliance with this program. It is one thing to have a law which prohibits something and to provide penalties which are to be suffered by those convicted of a violation of that law. That is part of what we consider to be the rule of law. It is a very different thing when you try to attain a very valid aim-an aim we can all support-through very vague threats. It is a different thing when you ask provincial governments, for example, to be prepared not to buy from a company because the Prices and Incomes Commission says that the company has violated this program. The government seems to feel that the end justifies the means and that this sort of thing has to be done in the national interest.
I do not think it is any exaggeration to say that most of the atrocities in history actually have been committed in the name of the public or the national interest. I say our democratic system requires more specific safeguards, and that we must take the rule of law seriously if we are going to preserve respect for the law, and if we are going to
4420	COMMONS
Government Administration preserve freedom. This kind of approach has serious implications for Canada because it can be very popular. A member of the government can appear popular if he seems prepared to bang somebody around, particularly a big business man or even a small one sometimes. You can be popular, but it is very dangerous. I do say if the government is prepared to use weapons such as this for good purposes, that is bad; but if the government is prepared to also use arbitrary actions to achieve something that is improper in itself, that is very bad indeed.
This brings me to the question of public information and the media. This is a delicate area in which Information Canada seems to pose a most direct threat, since the press has been proven a better judge of what in fact is information than the government has proven to be, whether by accident or design. We have had a succession of threats; a lecture to the press in London, a threat to have the mounted police look into the private lives of journalists, and a threat to lock the door at Radio Canada. These things reflect an attitude to the press which certainly makes me uncomfortable, and I think makes many journalists in Canada uncomfortable. This sort of thing may be popular. The vice-president of the United States, as well as the Prime Minister of Canada, has apparently found that the road to popularity lies in attacking the press and the media in this way. Just as the VicePresident of the United States, if I may say so, is creating great uneasiness there, the same sort of thing is creating uneasiness in our country.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
We should bear in mind the great power that governmental agencies have to control certain forms of the media. Radio stations and television stations are licenced only for short times. Therefore, the owners of these licences are bound to be nervous when anything that seems like a threat is involved. I think it is worth observation that this discomfort is not relieved by the convening in the other place of an inquiry into the media under the chairmanship of a former national director of the Liberal party. I believe he is known as the "Rainmaker". It is in this context that we have the suggestion, or at least the declared intention of the government, to establish Information Canada which I fear will be in fact "Manipulation Canada". In this context this is a very dangerous proposal. There is also related to this, the matter of the access of the government to the media. I 
DEBATES	March 5, 1970
think it would be useful for the CRTC to spell out the ground rules governing the conditions under which government statements should be allowed to preempt other programming on television, for example, by beating the audience to its knees. There seem to be no l'ules about this at the present time. Perhaps such a rule is particularly necessary in view of the new ruling regarding Canadian content and in view of the establishment by the government of a central propaganda agency authorized to use such vast and sophisticated techniques to tell the story on behalf of the Liberal government.
Perhaps the CRTC would consider some means of setting a rule concerning not only a minimum in respect of Canadian content but a maximum regarding government content or propaganda content. Mr. Speaker, propaganda and secrecy in this regard are two aspects of the same thing. They both relate to efforts to control public opinion. Both are methods which are always used by genuinely dictatorial governments. On the one hand, we have Information Canada coming along and, on the other hand, we have the virtual unlimited access of the government to networks. In addition, we have the secrecy and the refusal to give information. Then, there is the use of a vast number of task forces, the reports of which are kept secret. Of course, there is the well-known refusal to give information here in the House.
What is happening in respect of other institutions which traditionally were capable of standing up to the federal government? The provinces in Canada traditionally have provided some balance. After all, that is what the federal system is all about.
During recent years there has been some concern perhaps as to whether the federal government is strong enough to discharge its national responsibility. But there can be little doubt now concerning the direction in which we are headed. There can be little doubt now -and I say this advisedly-that the government is trying to beat the provinces to their knees by a fiscal squeeze. There can be little doubt that the government of Canada, through the white paper and other methods, is trying to create a preferred financial position for itself. It is one thing to ensure that we have a federal government with adequate powers to discharge its national responsibilities. It is another thing to create a situation in which there is a very real risk that an increasing number of provinces may become unable to discharge their constitutional responsibilities effectively and in which an increasing number
March 5, 1970	COMMONS
of provinces may be beaten into subserviency. Is there not a real danger in Canada today that fiscal restraint will turn into something like fiscal terrorism. I mentioned the white paper. If anybody thinks the federal government is above throwing its weight around in its relations with the provinces, he should ask himself how much real authority is left today to the legislature of Prince Edward Island.
It is against this sort of background that the playing down or downgrading of Parliament becomes even more significant. The things I have mentioned may seem to many people to be isolated instances, but really they are all part of a pattern. When we start to discuss Parliament in this context, we should recall the conception of Parliament apparently held by the majority of my friends opposite. This conception is that we have an election periodically; that following that election the government has a mandate and that between elections the only proper role of Parliament is to process whatever business the government may choose to place before Parliament. As I said before, and as I say again, the role envisaged for Parliament by most of my hon. friends opposite seems to be not very different from the role envisaged for the Chamber of Deputies by General de Gaulle.
At this point there is no need to review the rules debate except to note that the government was so intent on exercising authority that it used closure to bring in a rule that it cannot use.

This is a pretty good indication of the mentality of the members of this government and their attitude. In the discussions about Parliament, there has been much emphasis on efficiency and on the need for getting business done in this modern day. A great many rules that were formulated here to enable the opposition to dig in, and insist upon getting information, have been removed in the interest of getting the business done. I want to see Parliament efficient but I do not want to see it emasculated in the process. Parliament has been downgraded in a number of ways. There has been an increased volume of legislation which delegates very extensive powers to the Governor General in Council. This increased volume of such legislation has been a matter of concern for some time.
As a result of that concern, we had a report by a committee of this House on statutory
DEBATES	4421
Government Administration instruments. To my knowledge nothing has been done about that report. Not one step has been taken. Not one recommendation contained in that report has been implemented. The President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) keeps shaking his head. He looks quite natural when shaking his head in that direction. They are not easy of solution and they are not even easy of analysis. In the solution of all the issues that touch the daily lives of people, governments at all levels are required by the increasing consciousness of our society to take the initiative and to participate in the solution of the problems. It is no longer possible in modern society to think of solving any of the major problems by leaving them in the hands of private enterprise, private corporations or individuals in society. In every case, whether it is pollution, the quality of life, or the environment in which we live; whether it is the problem of education or of regional disparity, the question of bilingualism and national unity, the public authorities in the country, federal, provincial and municipal and the public treasuries of the country are necessarily and importantly involved.

Part of the problem, indeed I think the essence of it, is that this institution, the heart and centre of our democracy-if it is not that, it is not anything-is endangered not from without but from within. It is the Prime Minister of this country, next to Mr. Speaker himself, who should be the chief champion of the rights of Parliament. That is within the measure of his responsibility. However, even with all the great acting ability attributed to the Prime Minister by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis), 1 am sure there is 'no one in this country who can envisage him playing the role of the protector of this House and of the fullness of its rights and liberties. That is one act that he has never even endeavoured to put on.
Efforts to denigrate Parliament have been the earmarks of this government's dealings with this Parliament. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) has discussed the fiascos of the allocation of time debates. During recent months we have heard about what has happened to our committees: the government ignore their recommendations, pre-empt their recommendations, as when with undue and indecent haste they killled the Prince Edward Island causeway before the members of the transport committee have returned to Ottawa from making an on-the-spot investigation. The final stage was the directing of committees beforehand as to what to recommend, as in the case of the 18-year olds franchise.
Contempt of Parliament has been escalated, and is still escalating. Questions are ignored; the government refuses to disclose documents; questions asked by hon. members are evaded. Today, we have had scorn heaped upon the whole institution of the question period. It is clear that the asking of questions by opposition members is not something that is viewed by the government with pleasure, not something that they regard as important. It is conceivable in this era of the Park Avenue approach, an age when the image is the thing and manner is more important than matter, that something else may be substituted, that some process may be developed whereby questions as well as answers are manufactured in some sophisticated and costly way.

There is reason for thoughtful people to be concerned about what is taking place. Time was when governments actually appealed to the people in regard to what they were doing. Today the approach is what the Canadian people may be induced to believe that the government looks like or that the Prime Minister appears to be.
We are passing through a phase of austerity. But in the very midst of this we find that with lightning speed comes the announcement that the costly apparatus of Information Canada must be established forthwith. More millions and further regiments of public relations men will be hired to join the hundreds already employed in ministers' offices and at the Prime Minister's regional desks to disseminate news. When I asked the prime Minister a question about Information Canada some weeks ago, he indicated his relief in the importance of proper information. That is a very important adjective, and leads me to wonder who will judge what is proper and what is not proper. It is inconceivable to believe that it will be anyone but some government expert on public opinion management.
I do not think it is unrealistic to suggest that the glitter and glamour of 1968, the charisma of that exciting period, may have worn off or worn out by the time the next election comes, and so something else has to be ready. Information Canada and all the other intentions and manipulations referred to by the Leader of the Opposition in connection with the media are important matters. It is a strange thing that at a time when so many important operations of government, such as the Economic Council of Canada and many highly qualified people in the public service of Canada, even in the professional echelon, must be given the axe, we must rush with precipitous haste into the manufacture of government information.
We already have a situation where I believe there are more regional desks in the Prime Ministers office than there are seats in the House of Commons. That may be an exaggeration; perhaps they are not all desks but merely bureaux. We are told that in this new phase of participatory democracy the question period is to be diminished. Ministers have been told to stay away from the House. The caucus of the government party has been diminished in effectiveness, government members being told to meet not once a week but twice a month.
March 5, 1970
We have heard in recent weeks discussions, academic and otherwise, about the virtues and values of the presidential system. The Leader of the Opposition is very wise to get the point across that the presidential system that is conceived is not that of the United States, where the legislative arm is powerful, healthy, respected, and well able to discharge its duties in representing the people. Rather is it to be something that can be likened to the chamber of deputies under General de Gaulle. When I very carefully read the ministerial and prime ministerial statements about the kind of parliamentary body envisaged, I think it will be something much weaker even than the body that functioned in the third, fourth or fifth republic of France.
Therefore, it is important that we look now before it is too late and take stock of those measures, movements and intentions that would weaken this place. We are all accustomed as individual members of the House of Commons to being derided, to being made the butt-end of popular jokes. But when this institution itself is demeaned before the public, when more and more it seems to be irrelevant, it is time for us to take stock.
You do not have to be an evil man to destroy things that are good. All that is needed is a man with a distorted sense of values, to have a situation where precious things can quickly and perhaps imperceptibly disappear. Democracy, as we have discovered through the ages, is a frail flower. It cannot flourish in adversity; it has to be nurtured, it has to be nourished and it has to be protected. When he whom the people have given the greatest power and responsibility looks upon it as something that should be cribbed, cabined and confined, rather than enlarged and made more effective, then we are entering a climate in which it could wither and perish, a fate that none of us wants to see. Therefore, I appeal for support of this very perceptive motion so eloquently pleaded by the Leader of the Opposition.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the resolution put forward by the official opposition is a far-reaching one. It seems to deal with several things. Sometimes the motions brought forward by hon. members to the right seem to be rather double jointed, something like the title of their party. Although the title of my own party contains two words, at least its name is not a contradictory one. However that may be, I intend to confine my remarks to the part of the resolution which condemns the government for its arbitrary policies of secrecy and non-disclosure. We, for our part, also think the government is secretive. We have a proposal which we have already put forward as a means to cure part of that secretiveness.
I suppose the reason that I am speaking for our party at this moment is that I have a bill which deals with government secrecy, and how to avoid it. I refer to a bill in my name in respect of public access to government information. Of course, I am very much interested also in government information. It seems to me sometimes that government information and government secrecy are interchangeable terms. The Liberal government has been spending approximately $3 million a week on government information, for the most part so far as I can judge on publicity. It spends this money through the various departments and agencies of government, many of which are staffed by good friends of mine. They are very good fellows who, for the most part, are very anxious to do a good job in their fashion, but what a fashion to operate under! We have the report of the task force on government information. This is not the report of an opposition committee; it is the report of a government commission. That report strongly criticizes the government for its failure to provide government information sought by members of Parliament as representatives of the people of Canada.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
It is a fact that at this moment there are scores of motions for the production of papers on the Order Paper of the House, and we are
March 5, 1970

all familiar with the recital or the set phrases used by spokesmen for the government in denying members access to those papers. The aim of these motions which we and other members put forward is to gain access to the information which will reveal the basis of the decision of the government on matters of vital interest to the Canadian public because these decisions affect the lives of the people. To the extent that we are denied that information, there is a great degree of government secrecy in that area.
The task force report-again I say it was the report of the task force appointed by the present government-was most critical of the government on this point. It pointed out that while the government is spending an estimated $148 million a year to provide publicity, largely to say how good the government and its agencies are, it withholds the very basic facts which the public's representatives want to learn.
We think that government information is desirable when it helps the public. We do not think it is desirable when it is intended to help the government. We think that government information is useful when it is information such as is needed by veterans, pensioners or health and welfare recipients. We do not think it is needed in fields such as the competition between sections of the armed services. We do not think it is needed when it is used in such advertising, for example, as was recently indulged in by the Unemployment Insurance Commission, largely, it seemed to me, to glorify the UIC.
This is not the time to go into the matter of Information Canada, but may I say in passing that I very much doubt whether the addition of this new layer of government publicity apparatus to the existing layers in the departments is going to do much to clarify, make efficient or reduce the cost of what government information should do.
As to that part of the task force report dealing with government secrecy, which is contained in pages 25 to 34, it deals with a detailed examination and criticism of the hush-hush and secrecy now observed by the government. There are also some excellent comparisons between Canada's outmoded procedure in this area and those of other countries, notably Sweden. I should like to quote very briefly from the report which indicates the difference between the Swedish method of handling government information, that is allowing the public and opposition
Government Administration members access to governmental facts, and that of our country. It reads:
A full appreciation of the impact of the principle of open access can be gained only by giving some examples of the extensiveness of its operations. It applies, for example, to public documents kept by all sorts of administrative agencies, from government departments to police officers, administrative tribunals and local governments. Even parliament is under the rule; for instance, a citizen can demand to see the minutes of its committees. Moreover, anybody is entitled to ask for documents; he does not have to show that he has a legal interest in seeing them nor is he obliged to say for what purpose he wants them. To make sure that agencies do not purposely delay in answering a request, the Constitution of Sweden provides that a requested document shall be "made available immediately or as soon as possible", and the courts of Sweden in their judgments have taken this rule seriously.
A few months ago, the Southam news service, in making a survey which delved into government secrecy and the lack of access by the public to government information, said this:
Creation of a freedom of information act such as the one on the statute books in the United States would be a way to greater access of the public to government information.
The United States act of 1966 requires federal agencies to make available for public inspection and copying all final opinions, views, statements, policies and interpretations, staff manuals and the like. The act gives to the American people the right to challenge public officials in the courts if access is refused. Such an act for the Canadian scene has been proposed by me, and without burdening the House with any of its details I will simply say that I believe the adoption of some such measure would be a step toward ending the high degree of government secrecy which now prevails. We should do this mainly by making the House, through its committees and individual members, privy to almost everything which is going on in the government. We in our party prefer that course to what the Prime Minister appears to be doing at this time in dominating the cabinet, the caucus and Parliament and making his own direct line to the public.
May I say in conclusion that we support the motion of the official opposition, not that we really believe they would do differently from those in power whom they criticise but because we oppose what is being done now.

At the beginning of his remarks he put forward very precisely and perceptively a problem which is a continuing one in the development of governmental institutions, that tension which exists between any opposition and any government on the allocation of time, that tension and that balance which exist between the opposition's right to discuss and the government's right to present its legislation. He spoke about the difficulties and the necessity of adapting the traditional system to the needs of a modern age. This has always been a problem in British parliamentary institutions-it is not a new one. Over a hundred years ago Walter Bage-hot said:
The most imposing institutions of mankind are the oldest; and yet so changing is the world, so fluctuating are its needs, so apt to lose inward force, though retaining outward strength, are its best instruments, that we must not expect the oldest institutions to he now the most efficient. We must expect what is venerable to acquire influence because of its inherent dignity; but we must not expect it to use that influence so well as new creations apt for the modem world-
That is really the problem that faces us as parliamentarians,-the creation or adaptation of institutions to meet the modern world. What a speech the hon. member for York South could have made on that subject because of his experience and his sensitivity to political questions! Alas, he slid off into an easy attack on personalities, a smashing attack against style. I always find it rather puzzling that the hon. member for York South should be so much against style when he is so stylish himself and is married to such a stylish lady.
There were a few words in his speech about technocracy. Of course, nothing has been done in the past two years, he said. Regional development, the Criminal Code, the official languages act-an act on which both he and I worked-the committee system, tax reform, changes in foreign policy,-all this was forgotten; for him nothing has happened in the last two years. And then there was his long, rambling discussion about Denison Mines. I do not regret the speech the hon. member made; I regret very much the speech he did not make and could have made about a subject of permanent and continuing interest to members of this House.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) meandered about the subject, gingerly sidling up once in a while to an argument, as is his wont. I am puzzled by the Leader of the

Opposition. Once upon a time he was the leader of a government in Nova Scotia and there was not a great deal of activity by the independent members of that legislature. It was not so much a question of how closely that government approached parliamentary democracy but what kind of oriental despotism is exercised. I say "oriental" because it was way down east.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
This, Mr. Speaker, is a very curious motion indeed. I wonder if the Leader of the Opposition discussed it with the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). I am not surprised to see that that right hon. member is not here, because this motion, particularly in what it says at the end, is an attack on the general theme which has been sustained by the right hon. member for Prince Albert throughout his parliamentary career. This motion scorns the government because it "endangers the balance between the two structures of government-the executive and the representative." Two structures of government, Mr. Speaker, two different functions; one independent of the other, one looking at the other, one checking on the other. This is not a description of what has been traditionally the theme of parliamentary democracy, which regards the executive as a committee of the majority party, a committee of the House of Commons, uniting the representative and governing functions. This motion rejects the fundamental parliamentary principle of making the executive and representative power-cabinet and Commons-mutually dependent. It makes them independent opposed structures. There is quite a simple description for that theory of politics. It is called the separation of powers. That is the system they have in the United States. The introduction of that system is something which the right hon. member for Prince Albert has fought against throughout his parliamentary career, and therefore I am not surprised to find him not here to support it.
Even more curious, of course, is the way in which this motion automatically assumes that the opposition members alone are the representatives of the people. They represent the citizens. They often talk about the arrogance of the government in power. I can understand that. When you don't have power you rather resent those who have it. But what about the arrogance of the opposition? They ignore the majority of the people who voted for the government.

They, Mr. Speaker, are suffering from poverty. They are a poverty case. It is not a poverty of time, nor a poverty of opportunities. It is a poverty of ideas, a poverty of policies, a poverty of the capacity to communicate, and in the end, a poverty of leadership.

This is a democracy. In a democracy, the executive must be responsible to the elected representatives. Mr. Speaker, we have seen the roster system in operation. Nobody minds a minister being away from the House on government business, when he goes to Vancouver or overseas to study some problem. This is understandable. Every elected representative understands that point. But when Ministers deliberately stay behind the curtains, or run up to their offices, afraid to come into the House and answer questions about their responsibilities, that is not responsible government. That is not discharging the responsibilities of their office.
We hear members of the government talk about the fact that they were given a mandate. They were given a mandate to run the country-yes-but to be responsible in running it, to answer questions. We in the opposition have a mandate also, a mandate to scrutinize and to determine how legislation will be applied across the country. We heard some criticism this afternoon of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) for going across the country and attempting to explain the application of the White paper. Certainly, this is correct. He has a mandate to watch. He has a mandate to examine, and to examine very carefully how the government's proposed legislation will be applied across the country. He has a mandate to inform the people.
Some hon. member opposite quoted the press a great deal this afternoon. The press have a role in democracy. Their role is to be critical, to examine closely so as to inform the people of the exact application of the legislation and how the people will be affected.
The press, of course, today are groping and grasping for more and more power. They want the complete opposition out of the House. This is the way it is in the presidential system. The Leader of the Opposition isn't around. He is not in their debates. This is the way the press want it in Canada today. They want to take over the official role of the Official Opposition. That is their aim. That is their game.

speechtext:
I am not one of those members who speak very often in this Chamber. I have not had the opportunity to develop a speaking style and do not feel at ease when speaking in the House of Commons as do members of the opposition. It seems that when we are talking about the powers of Parliament, what we are really talking about is the quality of debate and the impact Members of Parliament can make on the general public: that is where the real power lies. This institution is not here for us to exercise power as our own right. We are here to exercise power as delegated by the people who elected us. If we are to have good debates and make our points clearly and forcibly to the public at large, the whole process must be dependent upon the exchange of ideas by members of the opposition and members of the government.
I came to this House in 1965, and it seems to me that the quality of debate has fallen off sharply since the election of 1968. The personnel on the government side have remained relatively constant; the personnel of the opposition, including the leadership, have changed. A logical analysis would lead one to believe there has been a decrease in the ability of the opposition to even oppose effectively, let alone initiate new ideas and concepts of government.
There has to be a two-way street. The House of Commons is not a forum for the government; it is basically constructed to provide a forum for the opposition. One of my frustrations as a backbencher is that the opportunities for me to speak in this Chamber are extremely limited because of our antiquated rules and the limited opportunities under those rules for members such as myself to participate. Until we have a sensible allocation of time rule in this House, government backbench members will have to pay the price; we will be unable to participate as much as we would like. It is necessary for the government to rule. For the government to do that, legislation must be passed and discipline exercised by the backbenchers in order that the greatest good can be accomplished.
I wish to say a few words about the committees system, which has been derided as a voice of the House of Commons by reason of the rules and attitude of opposition members. I get satisfaction from my committee work. I have been rather fortunate to be involved in
March 5, 1970

a number of issues in which there has been a great deal of excitement and the committees have had an opportunity to make genuine contributions.
I will use as an example the experience of the Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts Committee when dealing with the Company of Young Canadians. We held extensive hearings over a six-week period. We drafted a report which was submitted to the House of Commons. After considering the report, the government introduced legislation which in the main followed the recommendations which an all-party committee had made. I would point out to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) that very few party lines were drawn in that committee. The reason for this was that no party had given instructions to its members that they must take this position or that: the members were able to evolve the policy which was later accepted by the government. Certainly there were differences in detail; the members of the official opposition wished to wind up the CYC and some Liberal members voted with them, but the majority of the committee recommended that the operation should be continued under a new structure.
The Leader of the Opposition said something about removing participation from the council of the CYC. This is so, and the suggestion was included in the report but not as a strong recommendation. The report indicated that the system of participation of the CYC, by volunteers on the council, had not worked and was not likely to work in the future; therefore, if the Company was to be continued some other form of governing system had to be worked out. The government came up with the concept of a Crown corporation. This is a concept which has worked well in the past. Any Member of Parliament who has tried to get the CBC, the CNR, Air Canada or the Canada Council to change its mind once it has been made up under the Crown corporation system knows that these agencies have as much independence as they care to exercise.
I can think of one example which was raised some time ago in committee when the Canada Council had the temerity, according to the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale), to award Mr. Stanley Gray of Montreal a $5,000 scholarship. The members of the official opposition on that committee did everything they could to get the minister and the officials of the Canada Council to revoke the award. I am sure the Leader of the Opposition knows it was not done.
Government Administration
There are great powers available to members of committees if they wish to exercise them-which of course is the biggest risk of all. Many members on both sides of the House do not want to take this risk: it means1 exposing themselves, going out on a limb and taking your chances with the public. I feel the committee system that we now have is stronger than it has ever been. It is still evolving and getting stronger. Standing Order 65(8) sets out the powers of a standing committee. It reads:
Standing committees shall be severally empowered to examine and enquire into all such matters as-may be referred to them by the House, and, to>
report from time to time, and, except when the House otherwise orders, to send for persons, papers and records, to sit while the House is sitting, to sit during periods when the House stands adjourned, to print from day to day such papers and evidence as may be ordered by them, and to delegate to sub-committees all or any of their powers except the power to report direct to the House.
Any fair-minded person reading that Standing Order will realize that committees have a great deal of power and authority. It is a question of how much will and desire there is to exercise those powers. We have real problems in the committees system; I do not think anyone doubts that. At the present time there are 24 committees of the House of Commons; 19 standing committees, four joint committees and one which the House approved a few weeks ago, a Special Committee on Pollution comprising 15 members. This committee has yet to be established. This gives a total of 24 committees. They require a total of 595 Members of Parliament to staff them. There are 264 members in the House. Deduct 30 cabinet members, 16 Parliamentary Secretaries, 20 members for chairmen and 20 members on the opposition front benches who do not participate continuously in committee proceedings, and one is left with 178 members who are available for active committee duties-about 3.25 to a committee.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
Therefore, it seems to me that to ensure a much stronger committees system, three things should be done as a first step. The size of committees should be reduced to 12 members. We have experimented with this idea in the case of several special committees, such as the committee to consider the official languages bill. At present there are two committees of this size among our standing committees. This, it seems to me, would be a useful reform.
Second, we should reduce the number of committees from 19 to 14 or 15. Third,
4442	COMMONS
Government Administration research facilities should be made available to committees from the Library of Parliament research staff on a better basis. At present, members of this staff are being seconded to committees by reason of a somewhat dubious procedure. The problem is that once a committee obtains the services of a research person, it rarely lets him go. If the staff of the research section were increased, or if a separate division were set up, it would make it largely unnecessary to employ outside persons, often at considerable expense.
One of the things which might be changed is the method of appointment to committees, although I have no particular quarrel with the present method. It is my experience that no member has ever been pulled off a committee for voting against the government or for exposing weaknesses of administration. Tenure is always accorded. The government is well aware that if any member was yanked out of his place there would be a tremendous outcry. So members have as much freedom in committees as they want to take. That, of course, is the key phrase. Very often, though, members who might be doing useful work in [DOT]committee do not perform this work because they would prefer to see their names in the media. To be named by the media means to be spectacular and, to some extent, irresponsible because of the competition for media space among Members of Parliament. If we could forget the joy of seeing ourselves through the media we might be far better committee members and even far better Members of Parliament.
The Leader of the Opposition spoke about government hiding information. Anyone who looks at the amount of information being dredged up by committees cannot take such a charge seriously, particularly when under the current system officials of the departments, together with ministers, for extensive periods of time, are available for questioning. In addition, of course, it is possible for committees to send for papers and outside witnesses in connection with almost every subject which comes before them.
It is my opinion that Members of Parliament do not yet sufficiently appreciate the possibilities which the current rules provide. For some reason we are not prepared to do the necessary work in committees, though this would lead to greater knowledge and would obviously make us more effective Members of Parliament. It is not so much lack of information which concerns me; it is .the inability of members to make good use

of the information already available to them. This may be because our office facilities do not permit us to spend the time on this work that is necessary; the library research staff is overloaded. Nevertheless, in my opinion members do not take advantage of all the opportunities which now exist.
The House of Commons, and to a large extent the committees, are really a forum for the opposition. The government can take no blame or credit for a sparkling House of Commons, because the initiative must come from the opposition. The opposition has to provide the alternatives, the new approaches. I regret that when the record of this debate is read tomorrow it will probably be seen that the best speeches were made by members on the government side and not, unfortunately, by Members of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition.

There are significant differences between task forces and royal commissions; perhaps the most important is that neither statute or convention requires task forces to make public their reports.
There is a real danger in the secrecy which surrounds the surveys done by task forces.

When the government makes its policy decisions, it uses these reports. The public and Parliament cannot know on what facts the decision was based. It may be on factors known to all; or on secret information in the reports.
The public and Parliament cannot even know if the information was valid.
In one case it was not. After the Hellyer task force on housing reports, the government put a freeze on large public housing developments. It claimed that it did this because studies had shown that such projects had serious social, psychological and economic defects, and required further study.
It turned out later that the particular study involved had been only a pilot project designed to discover how such a study should be made. It has not surveyed a statistically meaningful group, just 100 public housing residents . . . the study was not nationally, provincially or even municipally representative. Of its use, its author said, "it's a good study-
Yet on the basis of that study the freeze was established.
This is far too dangerous a way to run a country. It opens the possibility-which cannot be checked by parliamentary opposition-that the decisions are made on inadequate or faulty research. It was another, quite unjust, effect; it provides masses of research, some of it undoubtedly of value, to experts outside government who may use it for their own purposes. This could be grossly unfair to persons and businesses surveyed, who do not have the information themselves.
Participatory democracy, if it is not to be cynical, must include feed-back as well as feed-in. The public and Parliament must be as well informed as the government if they are to challenge the government policy effectively. We have had the Prime Minister rise in this House and say, in answer to a question in respect of the Manhattan project, that it was not in any way, shape or form involved in any question of Canada's sovereignty in the north. Two days ago we heard over the radio from Newfoundland a statement by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) saying there must be a joint effort between his department and the Department of National Defence to protect our north because of the question raised by the Manhattan project in respect of Canadian


sovereignty in the north. This was a complete denial two days after the Prime Minister made his statement.
While we are talking about denials let us take another look at the Minister of Fisheries. He sat mute in his place despite the fact that legislation passed by the House provided him with the means of defending and protecting the Canadian fishing industry. This is the same minister who has gone around the country condemning his own government. The Prime Minister said not too long ago that there were going to be no loose-lipped statements made across this country by ministers. At one time it was an accepted principle that if a minister made a statement outside the House, unless he said he was speaking personally and on his own account, any statement he made outside the House was, in effect a statement of government policy.
Let us look at what the Minister of Fisheries has done to his own government. He has completely denied it. He has criticized and condemned his own government; yet he sits here and enjoys a seat on the executive of this country. He sits in the government with a Prime Minister who maintains he is going to maintain discipline within his cabinet. He is maintaining discipline all right! He is shoving the backbencher down, to use his own phrase, to a nobody. That is what he said we were, and that is what he is saying you are over there. You are nobody outside the House; you are nobody inside the House; you are nobody at caucus, and you are nobody in committee.
The Prime Minister is allowing the Minister of Fisheries to get away with a condemnation of his own government. Let me quote from a remark he made in British Columbia not too long ago:
I don't believe all that I read about dying lakes and sickening seas. Most of it is poppycock-written by novices who are reaching for headlines-
That is, anybody who questions pollution in this country or says anything about it is just a novice reaching out for headlines. That is what the minister said in British Columbia. Let me now read what the government has said-and the Minister of Fisheries is part of the government. I quote from the Throne Speech:
The evidence of past failure to rehabilitate our water resources is there for all to see-befouled water, despoiled beaches, rotting marine vegetation, and diminished fishing.
If this is not a complete contradiction by the Minister of Fisheries in respect of his own

cabinet and government, what is it? Where is this Prime Minister with his discipline? Where is he now in respect of his statement that no minister will go around the country making loose-lipped remarks about government policy? Here we have a minister completely condemning his own government, the members of which sit in silence when legislation of his House provides them with ways and means of protecting our fishermen. They do not answer. They contradicted their own Prime Minister two days after his back was turned.
Then we have the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) with his concern about the recognition of Red China. This is a dandy! Red China must be recognized. Mr. Speaker, at the beginning of this debate I heard a very precise quotation from Machiavelli by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield). But had he examined the book a little further he would have found that a worth-while prince, having encountered opposition to his plans, shall take good advice and shall continue his course of action in such a way that will make him loved and revered throughout the nation.
No one in this House would dare accuse me of ever kow-towing to either government edict, the Prime Minister's edict or anyone else's edict. I have always spoken however I thought right. I do not deny the statements I made 18 months ago. Hon. gentlemen opposite do not consider what is the great privilege of the House that they so fondly protect and want back again. One would imagine that prior to this administration this House was a most powerful body. It was not. It was a club. It was a luxurious and very exclusive club, but nevertheless it was a club. The committees had no meaning and this House had no meaning. We talked, not to each other but at each other. It was sad.
We discussed estimates, for example, and when the estimates were before us we could discuss any subject we desired. An hon. gentleman not now with us, from Fort William, regularly moved that the estimates be reduced from $700 million, $800 million or $100 million to $1. It was a vote of non-confidence. We were expected to be able to examine the estimates, but this was not the case. I do not deny for a minute that when this administration took over-and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) does not deny it either-the amount of policy decision-making was nil. It was recognized that government policy by and large was dictated by the elite, whether administrative, financial or other economic elite. It was the Prime Minister's determination to change the course of this Parliament.
