Mr. Speaker, I will wait until order is restored so as to be heard. I am pleased to be able to express my views on the motion presented by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), motion that is being discussed in the House today and deals with the government's policy of secrecy and non-disclosure of information they owe first to the House and secondly to the Canadian people.
We have noticed for a certain time that many ministers are absent from the House. Such absences may be motivated but it seems that the ministers of the most important departments are mainly the ones who are not in the house. In fact, I have not been able during the last four days to direct a question to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) because he was not in the House. I think that since this roster system was established, the order of attendance has not been respected. I suggest the ministers have been too often absent from the Houses during the last few days.
March 5, 1970	COMMONS DEBATES	4449
When the ministers are in the House, especially following a federal election, they give us fairly good answers, for they work zealously, as I have noticed since 1968. However, for the last six months, sound and valid replies are getting ever scarce and we can rightly complain about the information we have received to date.
For instance, when we ask questions about the C.B.C., the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) takes pleasure in saying that it is a crown corporation and that he does not want to interfere in its business. Yet, we know full well that the C.B.C., even taking into account the services it gives, spends ten times what a private concern would spend. In fact, the C.B.C. spends money extravagantly; this would not be tolerated by the most spendthrift, the richest private enterprise. Yet, the minister responsible for it has never brought up any of those problems.
It must surely come to this, as it did in the case of the Company of Young Canadians: some public man, such as the mayor of Montreal, or the chairman of the executive council of that city, or someone else who has nothing to do with federal politics, will levy serious charges against the C.B.C. or the federal government, based on information obtained from its police force or other sources of information. But, if damning evidence is produced, as in the case of the C.Y.C., the government may deem it advisable to take the necessary steps to hide the problem, to work its way around is, so that the accusers might not be proved right.
We notice that information is not given first in the House. In fact, we often get it from sources other than the legitimate one, that is the House of Commons.
I should also like to say a word about the committees. There is some talk about democracy in the committees, but the government in office as well as the other parties, would have a hard time convincing the government members to attend the sittings of the committees. Why? Because, in spite of the fine promises made by our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) advocating democracy, the members cannot play their part as representatives of the people because no information is available to them.
The government makes use of its majority to eliminate witnesses, as it happened with regard to certain suggestions which I had made. At the time my witnesses were not allowed to appear because the government was afraid of them. In that instance, the
Government Administration majority was used to conceal as much information as possible and which is worse, on two occasions, committees adopted a report which the government refused to accept later on.
There is an increasing tendency to conceal facts, figures, in short everything. I would not want us some day to become totally useless in the House and in the committees. That is why I thought it advisable to say a few words on the motion moved by the Leader of the Opposition.
Every time Parliament has been faced with a problem, instead of asking hon. members to study it in detail, to undertake research in order to solve it, the government has deemed necessary to appoint royal commissions. If any hon. member wants the information, I shall be happy to provide it in a minute. There is one closing observation that should be made, Mr. Speaker, in connection with the way of the House operates. At the present time, out of around 155 to 160 days in the parliamentary calendar, about 40-certainly 25 per cent of the time-are designated as days on which the opposition either control entirely the subject matter of the debate, or are at liberty to discuss as freely as they wish any subject in connection with which they may wish to criticize the government. I refer to the number of days allotted to the opposition on which they control the subject matter of the debate; to the budget debate; and also to the Throne Speech debate in which opposition members participate fully, criticizing the government on a whole range of subjects.
In addition, there is provision for setting aside time for emergency debates, which is always an opposition prerogative. On top of that, there is the time occupied by the opposition during private members' hour. The opposition is also on its feet for about 95 per cent of the time allotted to the question period. Then, of course, there is the system under winch time in any given debate is allotted. As we know, there is always a desire in any given debate to recognize opposition members and consequently there is more participation by opposition members than by members on the government side. Accordingly, as a matter of simple mathematics, the time taken by opposition members in directing themselves to the subjects being considered is perhaps double the time taken by government members.

Mr. Speaker, I acknowledge my debt to you and the previous speaker for the opportunity of making one or two very brief observations in this debate. It would have been interesting to spend the remaining seven or eight minutes dealing with some of the comments of the last two speakers. Suffice it to say that it is interesting to recall the time spent in this House by the government in forcing upon this nation an iniquitous amendment under the Excise Tax Act dealing with enabling legislation to tax airline tickets, only to have the government a few weeks later crawling back into the House and saying, "After all, fellows, we do not want to do anything about this until next year." Therefore, it means nothing to me to hear people talking about time being wasted in this House.
I want to speak for a minute or two about the type of situation that is evolving and the trend that is developing in this House as it has a direct effect upon the people. I have in mind the people of Canada who sent us here. Apropos of that, it is not necessarily to the backbenchers that we are speaking. They understand what we are saying. We are speaking to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) of this country, and he had better listen because the rest of the people of the country have been listening to us and are becoming very concerned.
The point I want to raise in the few minutes I have available to me is the very undesirable consequence of the government keeping unto itself bits and pieces of information that are vital if our economy and our people are not to suffer adversely from policy decisions made from time to time by the government. As much as two years ago I began asking questions in this House, along with my colleagues, about the economic impact of base consolidation and reductions in defence spending as a direct result of government policy. On every occasion these questions were asked there came back assurances from the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cadieux) that no precipitate action would be taken without prior consultation and discussion with the economic units involved-the provinces, cities and towns.
Government Administration
What do we have? Without reading them, but going back to July 18, 1969, one can find comments at page 11341, July 24 at page 11537, and as recently as December 8 at page 11697 of Hansard. Let me quote one brief comment. I am not taking it completely out of context, but slightly, without changing the essence of what the Minister of National Defence had to say. He said that so far the intent is that there shall not be any further change in the situation in the Maritime provinces. The minister was responding to questions not only from myself but other hon. members in this Chamber about the economic impact of changes in defence policy.
What do we have as a result of this wide open policy of communication with the civic units involved? What do we have as a result of the policy intention of the government and the direct pragmatic and practical procedures and steps to be followed? We have seen within the last three months the closing of Fairey Aviation without prior consultation; we saw the closing last night of EMI Cosser in Dartmouth without prior consultation; and we have heard rumoured very seriously this week that the Dockyards Trade and Labour Council in Halifax, as a result of the intention of the government, is to start reducing staff by laying off several hundred civilian employees.
If it is necessary to do these things, it is incumbent upon the government to go to the economic units involved and tell them its reasons. If the government will not tell us here in the House of Commons what is going on, at least it should go to the economic unit that is most directly affected, that is to say, the city, the village, the town or the province. The government should talk to the civic and community leaders in those places telling them well in advance what it intends to do. But it has not done that, and it has no intention of doing that. This has been made patently clear.
The tendency to withhold information is leaving, not only the members of the opposition but I am sure many, many backbenchers with a feeling of frustration. Something serious is happening: people are being left with the impression that they can no longer believe what they are being told by the treasury benches of this government. It may well be that the treasury benches of this government are not advised by the Prime Minister of his intentions. I suspect that in no small measure that is the reason for the situation. He advises them in many cases in his office or through the medium of the press.

One member of the treasury benches employs a student to read the newspapers and tell him what his colleagues and the gov-erment are doing. Is that any way to run the government of this country? If I were that member, I would have long since resigned. I shall come back to one of my serious fears about the tendency to withhold or hide information. We have suspicions in respect of the actions of the government, for instance, under the austerity program. Indeed, a year or so ago we were told by the Minister of National Defence and others that there would have to be extensive lay-offs of civilian employees in the Department of National Defence, probably as many as 5,000.
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that not only in the case of these civilian employees but in all matters directly affecting individuals who have wives and families and who live under a threat, belief or understanding that at some point in the future somebody may-not positively will-say to them, "I am sorry; you are no longer required", it is incumbent upon the government to stand up, accept its responsibility and go not only to this Chamber-we are prepared to accept being placed in the background-but to the civic bodies affected, the towns and cities, and lay bare their plans.
Mr. Speaker, I support this motion. The hon. gentleman from Halifax proposed it in all seriousness; it was not put forward lightly. This matter was raised in our caucus which happens to meet in a forum of free expression, unrestricted and unfettered. The motion has been put forward seriously and I suggest to the government and its backbenchers that they indeed take it seriously.
